extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary readers, and critics interested in 19th-century American literature and craft
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted craft-and-judgment criteria from a reflective literary-memoir: compact guidelines and evaluative observations about authorship, style, originality, seriousness, and the relation of an author's life to their work. Useful for writers and critics assessing literary quality and authorial character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and absence of posing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nothing could have been further from the behavior of this very great man than any sort of posing... he was no more tacitly than he was explicitly didactic.", (about Hawthorne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authors whose manner and speech avoid affectation or self-promotion; authenticity in personal encounter is a marker of authentic artistry. Anti-pattern: an author who surrounds himself with a "subtle ether of potential disapprobation" and implicitly sets himself up as an example, thereby provoking discomfort in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character reflected in the work
rubrics_metrics.description: "I knew that men were his books... though I myself cared for books so much, I found it fit and fine that he should care so little."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider an author's personal demeanor and kindness as relevant evidence for judging their writing: how they comport themselves (modesty, equality, sincerity) can illuminate the spirit behind their work. Example: Hawthorne's cordial, modest presence harmonized with his romances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive, inimitable individual difference
rubrics_metrics.description: "We are always finding new Hawthornes, but the illusion soon wears away... he had some peculiar difference from them, which, by and-by, we shall no doubt consent must be his difference from all men evermore."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness includes an irreducible personal difference that imitators lack; beware of mistaking stylish imitation for authentic voice. Test: does the work sustain a sense of unique perspective beyond fashionable traits?

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of large moral/philosophical problems (narrative resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding the Marble Faun: "Everybody was reading it, and more or less bewailing its indefinite close... as far as the problem of evil was involved, the book must leave it where it found it. That is forever insoluble."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a work treats deep, insoluble problems (evil, fate, suffering): whether it illuminates the problem even if it cannot solve it, and whether its formal choices (e.g., an "indefinite close") are artistically justified rather than merely unsatisfactory. Scoring note: recognizing a problem's insolubility can be valid; the criterion is whether the work engages it with honesty and artistic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simple, lucid appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Emerson had "reached the dense intelligence of his fellow-men after a whole lifetime of perfectly simple and lucid appeal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity of expression and lucid thought are virtues; writing that communicates complex thinking simply is a sign of mastery. Anti-pattern: obscurity masquerading as profundity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical discernment must transcend personal fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Emerson had, in fact, a defective sense as to specific pieces of literature; he praised extravagantly, and in the wrong place... and he failed to see the worth of much that was fine and precious beside the line of his fancy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism requires steady judgment not merely the praise of what pleases the critic's own taste. Evaluate works on their merits, not solely on how they fit a critic's whim or ideological preference. Anti-pattern: overpraising the fashionable or personally resonant at the expense of other qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature that exposes social falsity has lasting power
rubrics_metrics.description: On Thoreau's Walden: "he more clearly showed the hollowness, the hopelessness, the unworthiness of the life of the world than Thoreau did in that book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that keenly reveal societal folly or spiritual hollowness can have enduring significance even if they offer no practical solution. Evaluate for clarity of vision, prophetic force, and moral seriousness rather than for prescriptive practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial life and heroism affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoreau's moral actions (aiding John Brown, suffering in prison) — "this inevitable heroism of his that, more than his literature even, made me wish to see him and revere him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider biographical conduct and public courage as factors that shape readers' esteem and interpretation of a writer's work. Note: this is a reception criterion (how readers value a writer), not a pure aesthetic test of textual quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness of poetry over mere pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: On giving "a pleasant hour to poetry": "A pleasant hour to poetry!... I should have thought that a proof of inferior quality in the work; I should have preferred anxiety, anguish even, to pleasure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High poetry is judged by its moral and emotional gravity—its capacity to unsettle, challenge, or provoke—rather than by creating easy, comfortable pleasure. Anti-pattern: equating mere entertainment or light pleasure with poetic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid performative Bohemian pose; prefer substantive originality
rubrics_metrics.description: On Bohemia and the Saturday Press: the pose was "a vain and unprofitable one..." and much of the Bohemian affectation disappointed the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of affectations (cynical postures, deliberate offensiveness, shock-value) that substitute for sustained craftsmanship. Value genuine innovation and generosity to neglected talents over theatrical rebellion. Example anti-patterns: spasmic one-word paragraphs, shock as artistic badge without underlying workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty is a means, not an end; craft completes liberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Whitman: "He was a liberating force... but liberty is never anything but a means, and what Whitman achieved was a means and not an end... his verse seems to me not poetry, but the materials of poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for formal or ideological liberation (breaking conventions) should be coupled with attention to craft and form. Distinguish between a liberating impulse and completed artistic work: materials of poetry must be shaped into poetry. Practical test: does experimentation culminate in formally satisfying and expressive results?

rubrics_metrics.name: Local recognition and sustained responsibility deepen the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: "The unrecognized celebrity probably has his mind quite as much upon himself... It involves the sense of responsibility, which cannot be too constant or too keen. If it narrows, it deepens; and this may be the secret of Boston."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the social context of an artist: a connected local literary community can foster responsibility, seriousness, and depth in work. Anti-pattern: complete anonymity that fosters self-absorption; counterbalance with national fame that erodes neighborhood accountability.
